Even this website is something interesting to talk about - at least to me.For the past 6 months or so I've been fairly enamored with using LLMs to build (mostly) software stuff. I've always enjoyed building things in the world of general internet-related technologies, and for the last half of my professional career I was either building, supporting, or monitoring enterprise tooling and platforms across several industries.I always enjoyed stumbling across a nice batteries-included tutorial to build some cool thing in docker, or some vendors detailed installation for their community-edition or self-hosted option.I, early-on, installed a proxmox server in my basement, and used portainer to make building platforms and docker-based applications super convenient.But now, using LLMs that are aware, by definition, of how everything is built and how they work, dynamic and mostly right tutorials are at our fingertips for ANYTHING - and simply by asking for it.
This site is constructed in Obsidian, and using an Obsidian plug-in written, coincidentally, by a fellow I know from the lab I am involved with at UofL, Nathan George, the Obsidian vault containing these pages can be exported as a complete website.Once the pages are exported locally, a typical static site publishing workflow is used to: make updates to a repo push that repo to github use github pages to 'publish' those pages to a publicly accessible URL
Here is that repo and here is an explanation / setup page I asked Claude to write for me when I was done.

item.title: 03 - reflections
item.description: Seven Signs, Seven Sacraments Scripture Focus: John 1–2Can you name all seven "signs" in John's Gospel? What sacrament(s) do you think each one points to?One of the most luminous contributions Dr. Bergsma makes in this course is the recovery of a patristic insight that the modern Church is only now rediscovering in full: that the seven miraculous signs John records in his Gospel are not simply demonstrations of divine power, but sacramental signposts — each one pointing toward one or more of the Seven Sacraments of the Catholic Church. John himself tells us that his selection is deliberate and purposeful: "Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples that are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may come to believe" (John 20:30–31). He chose seven. The number is not accidental.What follows is a synthesis of the seven signs with their sacramental correspondences, drawing on the logic of John's Gospel and the tradition of Catholic biblical interpretation.Sign 1 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine (John 2:1–11) Sacrament: The Eucharist (and Matrimony)The first sign establishes the pattern for all that follow. Jesus transforms the water of the old purification rites — water used for Jewish ceremonial washings — into an abundance of the finest wine. The quantity is staggering: six stone jars holding twenty to thirty gallons each. This is not a modest top-up of the refreshments. It is an overwhelming superabundance of the new, poured out in place of the old.The Eucharistic connection is primary: Jesus, the true Bridegroom, provides the good wine that the human bridegroom could not. At the Last Supper, He will take the cup and declare it His Blood — the cup of the New Covenant, the "good wine kept until now" (John 2:10) in its ultimate fulfillment. The scene at Cana is the first act of what the Upper Room completes.The setting — a wedding — also gives this sign a secondary Matrimonial dimension. Jesus sanctifies and elevates the marriage covenant by His presence and by His first act of glory. The Catechism teaches that Christ's presence at Cana confirms the goodness of marriage and inaugurates the wine of the messianic age (CCC 1613).Sign 2 — Healing of the Royal Official's Son (John 4:46–54) Sacrament: Anointing of the SickThe official comes to Jesus in anguish — his son is near death. Jesus heals the boy at a distance, without touching him, through a word spoken in response to the father's desperate faith. "Go; your son will live" (John 4:50). The man believes the word and departs, and the healing is confirmed.This sign points to the Sacrament of Anointing of the Sick, which the Catechism describes as the sacrament by which "the Church entrusts the sick to the suffering and glorified Lord" (CCC 1499). Like the official, the Church brings the sick to Christ with faith, not with sight, trusting in the power of His word to heal body and soul. The distance between Jesus and the dying child in John 4 mirrors the mystery of sacramental grace — it operates not by physical proximity but by the power of Christ's word mediated through the Church.Sign 3 — Healing of the Paralytic at Bethesda (John 5:1–15) Sacrament: Penance and ReconciliationThe paralytic has lain helpless for thirty-eight years. Jesus heals him with a command — "Rise, take up your mat and walk" (John 5:8) — and then, when He finds the man later in the Temple, speaks words that reveal the deeper dimension of what has happened: "See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you" (John 5:14).The connection to the Sacrament of Reconciliation could not be more explicit. The healing is not merely physical; it is bound up with the forgiveness of sin. Jesus is presented here as the one with authority to release both physical and spiritual paralysis. In the Sacrament of Penance, the priest acts in persona Christi, speaking the same liberating word to souls paralyzed by sin: you are forgiven, rise and walk. Sin no more.Sign 4 — The Feeding of the Five Thousand (John 6:1–15) Sacrament: The EucharistThe fourth sign is the most explicitly Eucharistic of all, and John makes certain we cannot miss it. Jesus takes bread, gives thanks (εὐχαριστήσας, the very word from which "Eucharist" derives), and distributes it to the multitude. He then delivers the Bread of Life Discourse (John 6:22–71), in which He states with unmistakable clarity: "my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink" (John 6:55). Many disciples depart at this teaching because it is too hard. Jesus does not soften it.The feeding on the hillside is a preview and a preparation for the Eucharistic institution at the Last Supper. Both the bread distributed in John 6 and the Eucharistic loaf share the same fourfold action that marks every Eucharist: Jesus takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it. Where the Cana miracle points to the Eucharistic cup, the Feeding of the Five Thousand points to the Eucharistic bread.Sign 5 — Walking on Water (John 6:16–21) Sacrament: Baptism (and Confirmation)The disciples are caught in a storm at night, far from shore, straining at the oars. Jesus comes to them, walking on the water — across the very waters of chaos and darkness that, in the Old Testament imagination, represent the forces hostile to God and to human life. His words of self-identification — "It is I" (ἐγώ εἰμι, "I AM") — are the divine name revealed to Moses at the burning bush.This sign points toward Baptism: Jesus as the master of the primordial waters, the One who crosses the sea of death and emerges on the other side. The Christian who is baptized enters those same waters and emerges with Christ — passing through death and darkness into new life. The crossing of the sea is one of the great Baptismal types of the Old Testament (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and Jesus recapitulates and fulfills it. Some also see here a pointer to Confirmation — the strengthening of the disciples against fear and storm by the presence of the Spirit-filled Christ.Sign 6 — Healing of the Man Born Blind (John 9:1–41) Sacrament: BaptismThe sixth sign is among the richest baptismal passages in all of Scripture. A man who has been blind from birth — who has never seen the light — is healed when Jesus makes clay, anoints his eyes, and sends him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. The man washes and comes back seeing.Every element of this sign resonates with Baptismal theology. The clay made from earth and spittle echoes Genesis 2:7 — God forming man from the dust of the ground. The anointing of the eyes prefigures the anointing with chrism at Baptism. The washing in the Pool of Siloam — whose name John translates as "Sent" (ἀπεσταλμένος), pointing to the one who is sent from the Father — is the sacramental bath that opens the eyes to divine light. It is for good reason that the early Church called Baptism photismos — enlightenment, illumination. The man born blind is the paradigmatic image of what Baptism accomplishes: to be plunged into the waters and to emerge seeing for the first time.Sign 7 — The Raising of Lazarus (John 11:1–44) Sacrament: Baptism (and Anointing of the Sick)The seventh and greatest sign is the raising of Lazarus, which functions as the culminating preview of the Resurrection itself. Jesus stands before the sealed tomb — "Lazarus, come out!" (John 11:43) — and a man four days dead walks out into the light, still bound in his burial cloths.The primary sacramental resonance is with Baptism: the passage from death to life, the emergence from the tomb-womb of the waters into the light of the risen Christ. In the early Church, baptisteries were often constructed in octagonal shapes symbolizing the eighth day — the day beyond the seven-day week, the day of the Resurrection, the day Lazarus prefigures. To be baptized is to be Lazarus — called out of the tomb by the voice of the Lord, unbound, and sent into the community of the living.The secondary resonance with Anointing of the Sick is also real: the sacrament the Church has always associated with the dying and the dead, the anointing that prepares the soul for its passage from this world to the next. Jesus delays His coming to Lazarus by two days — long enough to ensure the man is unmistakably dead — so that the glory of God might be fully revealed. The sacrament does not always restore physical life. But it always opens onto the eternal life that Lazarus's resurrection signifies.The Prologue of John states that "the darkness has not overcome [the light]" (John 1:5). What do you think John means by this? What might he be trying to tell us about Jesus' life and ministry as a whole?John 1:5 is a thesis statement for the entire Gospel. Every episode that follows — every sign, every controversy, every moment of misunderstanding and rejection, and ultimately the Passion itself — must be read in its light. To understand this verse is to hold the interpretive key to the whole of John's theological vision.The Double Meaning: A Deliberate AmbiguityThe Greek verb that most English translations render as "overcome" is κατέλαβεν (katelaben), from the root καταλαμβάνω (katalambanō). It is a word with a rich semantic range, and John almost certainly intends both of its primary meanings simultaneously.On the one hand, katalambanō means to overtake, seize, or overpower. On the other hand, it means to comprehend, understand, or grasp. Both meanings are operative in John 1:5, and this is not accidental. John is the most theologically self-conscious author in the New Testament, and his use of polyvalent language — words and images that carry multiple meanings at once — is one of the defining characteristics of his literary style.Read in the first sense, verse 5 is a cosmic declaration: the darkness has not overpowered the light. The forces of evil, sin, and death — what John elsewhere calls the ruler of this world (John 12:31; 14:30) — have not been able to extinguish the divine light that entered the world in the person of Jesus Christ.Read in the second sense, verse 5 is a statement about incomprehension: the world did not understand the light. John 1:10–11 develops this second meaning explicitly: "He was in the world, and the world came to be through him, but the world did not know him. He came to what was his own, but his own people did not accept him." The darkness cannot even comprehend what it is up against.John holds both meanings together because they interpret each other. The world's failure to understand Jesus is itself a form of its failure to overcome Him. The powers of darkness think they are defeating the light when they send Jesus to the Cross. They cannot understand what they are looking at. And precisely in that incomprehension, the light triumphs.The Cross as the Apparent Victory of DarknessThis verse functions as a proleptic anticipation of the Passion narrative. If you read John's account of the arrest, trial, and crucifixion of Jesus without the lens of verse 1:5, it can appear to be a story of darkness winning. The authorities plot, Judas betrays, the crowd shouts for crucifixion, the soldiers nail the light of the world to a cross at a place called the Skull. The darkness seems to have seized its prey at last.But John presents the Passion in an entirely different key. In his Gospel, the Cross is not the defeat of Jesus — it is His exaltation. He speaks of being "lifted up" (John 3:14; 8:28; 12:32) using a verb that means both physical elevation and glorification. The "hour" that Jesus keeps deferring throughout the Gospel — "My hour has not yet come" (John 2:4) — turns out to be the hour of His death, which is simultaneously the hour of His glory (John 12:23: "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified").Darkness rushes upon the light and finds that it cannot hold it. The tomb is sealed. Soldiers stand guard. And on the third day, the stone is rolled back and the light of the Resurrection blazes out — not despite the darkness that tried to contain it, but through it.The Ongoing TensionIt would be a mistake to read John 1:5 as a statement about a battle already over. The tension between light and darkness runs through the entire Gospel and, the Church teaches, through the entire history of the world until Christ returns. Every soul is, in some sense, Nicodemus coming to Jesus at night — aware of the light, drawn toward it, but not yet fully emerged from the darkness.John's declaration that the darkness has not overcome the light is not a smugly triumphalist claim. It is a promise, spoken at the threshold of the Gospel, to sustain the reader through everything that follows: the misunderstandings, the rejections, the betrayals, the suffering, and the silence of the tomb. The light has not been put out. It never will be.In John 2:21, why does Jesus speak of "the temple of his body"? By using this phrase, what is He revealing about His identity?The Cleansing of the Temple in John 2:13–22 is one of the most theologically charged scenes in the entire Gospel, and the verse at its center — "he was speaking about the temple of his body" (John 2:21) — is among the most direct claims to divine identity in all of Scripture.The Temple and the Presence of GodTo grasp what Jesus is claiming when He identifies His body as the Temple, we must first understand what the Temple was. It was not merely a religious building or a site of ritual observance. It was the dwelling place of the divine Presence — the one location on earth where heaven and earth intersected, where God's glory (kavod, Shekinah) was concretely, tangibly present among His people.The history of God's presence among Israel follows a trajectory: the Tabernacle in the wilderness, where the glory-cloud descended and filled the tent (Exodus 40:34); the Temple of Solomon, into which the glory of the Lord entered at its dedication so powerfully that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11); the exile, during which Ezekiel saw the glory depart from the Temple (Ezekiel 10–11); and the return from exile, after which the Second Temple stood — magnificent in its reconstruction under Herod, but conspicuously, achingly, without the divine Shekinah. The glory had not returned.Into this context of absence and longing, John announces in his Prologue: "The Word became flesh and dwelt [tabernacled] among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). The glory has returned. It has not returned to the stone Temple on the hill. It has come to dwell in a human body — the body of the eternal Son.The Claim of John 2:21When Jesus says "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19), His hearers understand Him to be making a grandiose and offensive claim about the Jerusalem Temple — the largest and most magnificent building most of them had ever seen, forty-six years in the building. Their incomprehension is understandable.But John, with his characteristic technique of dramatic irony, tells us what Jesus actually meant: He was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:21). This is one of the most compressed and explosive theological statements in the New Testament. Unpacked, it contains at least four distinct claims about Jesus's identity:First, Jesus is identifying Himself as the true dwelling place of God — the fulfillment of everything the Temple was meant to be. He does not come to worship in the Temple as one among many. He comes as the One to whom the Temple pointed and in whose presence it becomes obsolete. As the Catechism states: "Jesus acted as the One who is master of the Temple, which points to His divine identity" (CCC 586).Second, Jesus is claiming sovereignty over His own death and resurrection. "In three days I will raise it up" — not it will be raised, but I will raise it. He is not speaking as a victim awaiting an execution. He is speaking as the One who lays down His life and takes it up again by His own authority (John 10:18). This is a claim only God could make.Third, the identification of His body as the Temple is a key to understanding the theology of the Eucharist and the Church. If Jesus is the Temple — the place where God dwells — then where His body is present, there is the divine Presence. The Eucharist, in which His Body and Blood are truly present, makes every church building in the Christian world a site of the divine Shekinah in a way the Jerusalem Temple never was. And the body of each believer, incorporated into Christ through Baptism and nourished by the Eucharist, becomes itself a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).Fourth, the phrase "in three days" points unmistakably forward to the Resurrection. John tells us that only after the Resurrection did the disciples understand what Jesus had meant (John 2:22). The entire exchange at the Temple is written from the vantage point of Easter morning — from the perspective of those who have seen the destroyed temple of His body raised on the third day and who now understand, with the luminous clarity of retrospection, the full weight of what He had said.The New Temple Theology of JohnThis passage is the fulcrum on which John's entire Temple theology turns. John 4:21–24 — Jesus telling the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when worship will be "in Spirit and truth", neither on Mount Gerizim nor in Jerusalem — continues the same logic. The Jerusalem Temple is being superseded not because it was wrong, but because it was a sign pointing toward what has now arrived. The sign yields to the reality it signified. In Jesus, the glory has returned — and it has come to stay.

item.title: 04 - practical application
item.description: Seven Signs, Seven Sacraments Scripture Focus: John 2:1–12Reread the account of the Wedding at Cana (John 2:1–12). In light of your own prayer life, consider the exchanges that take place between Our Lady, Jesus, and the servants. Be honest; when you are in need, do you turn to God, or something else? When you pray, do you find yourself constantly trying to problem-solve on God's behalf? As you read through this passage, pay close attention to Mary's humility, the swift obedience of the servants, and the trust that the steward puts in Jesus. Write down two or three practical ways you could apply what you see to your own relationship with the Lord. As you go about your week, return to your list and reflect on what you wrote.As you read the passage, pay close attention to each of the three human figures in this scene and what they model for us:Our Lady — She notices the need before anyone asks her to. She brings it simply and without drama to Jesus. She does not tell Him what to do, or how, or when. She presents the need, receives what sounds like a refusal, and trusts Him anyway. Her instruction to the servants is her instruction to us: "Do whatever he tells you."The Servants — They are told to fill stone purification jars with water — an ordinary, unheroic task. They fill them to the brim. No half-measures. Then they are told to draw some out and take it to the headwaiter — trusting a command that makes no rational sense. They obey immediately, without waiting to understand. And the miracle happens in the act of obedience.The Headwaiter — He tastes the wine and is astonished at its quality, but he does not know where it came from. He receives the gift of Christ without fully understanding its source. Only the servants know. This is a portrait of the many in the Church who receive the grace of the sacraments without grasping the full mystery of what they have been given.Mary, our Mother and our Queen, you who stood at the wedding feast and noticed our need before we knew to ask — intercede for us now as we open the Word of your Son. Teach us your humility, your trust, your swift surrender. And in the words you spoke to the servants, speak also to us: "Do whatever he tells you." Amen.New American Bible, Revised Edition (NABRE)The Wedding at Cana1 On the third day there was a wedding in Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. 2 Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding. 3 When the wine ran short, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine." 4 Jesus said to her, "Woman, how does your concern affect me? My hour has not yet come." 5 His mother said to the servers, "Do whatever he tells you."6 Now there were six stone water jars there for Jewish ceremonial washings, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. 7 Jesus told them, "Fill the jars with water." So they filled them to the brim. 8 Then he told them, "Draw some out now and take it to the headwaiter." So they took it.9 And when the headwaiter tasted the water that had become wine, without knowing where it came from (although the servers who had drawn the water knew), the headwaiter called the bridegroom 10 and said to him, "Everyone serves good wine first, and then when people have drunk freely, an inferior one; but you have kept the good wine until now."11 Jesus did this as the beginning of his signs in Cana in Galilee and so revealed his glory, and his disciples began to believe in him.12 After this, he and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples went down to Capernaum and stayed there only a few days.When I am in need, my first instinct is to turn to...A way I find myself trying to problem-solve on God's behalf in prayer:What I notice about Mary's posture in this scene:What I notice about the servants' obedience:Two or three concrete ways I will apply what I see in this passage to my relationship with the Lord this week:1.2.3.Return to this page at the end of the week and reflect on what you wrote above.What happened when I tried to apply these things?What did I learn about my own prayer life?

item.title: 02 - review
item.description: Seven Signs, Seven Sacraments Scripture Focus: John 1–2True or False: Jesus is the new Isaac and the new Moses. a. True b. False This question is an invitation to precision — and precision in biblical typology matters enormously, because misidentifying the type obscures the theological truth the sacred author is actually communicating. In Episode 2, Dr. Bergsma draws our attention to the specific typological identities that John's Gospel is constructing in chapters 1 and 2. They are not Moses and Isaac. They are Adam and the Bridegroom.Jesus as the New AdamThe signal is sounded in the very first words of the Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1). This is not accidental phrasing. The opening words of John's Prologue — ἐν ἀρχῇ (en archē), "in the beginning" — are the precise words that open the Septuagint's translation of Genesis: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). John is announcing, before a single episode of Jesus's ministry has been narrated, that what we are about to read is a new Genesis. The story of Jesus is the story of a new creation.Where the first Adam was formed from the dust of the old creation, the new Adam — the Word made flesh — enters the world from eternity itself. Where the first Adam failed in the garden, succumbing to the serpent and plunging all creation into darkness, the new Adam will succeed. He is, as St. Paul will later articulate in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, the last Adam — the one who undoes what the first Adam did and recapitulates all of human history in Himself.John reinforces this Adam typology throughout chapters 1 and 2. The seven-day structure that Dr. Bergsma identifies in John 1:1–2:11 — in which the narrative unfolds across a series of successive days — is designed to evoke the seven days of creation in Genesis 1. Jesus does not simply teach about a new creation; He embodies and inaugurates it.Jesus as the Eschatological BridegroomAlongside the Adam typology runs the Bridegroom typology, which reaches its first climax at the Wedding of Cana. The scene is immediately recognizable to any reader formed in the Old Testament as a betrothal type-scene. In the patriarchal narratives, a man journeys to a foreign land, meets a woman, and a marriage covenant follows. Isaac's servant meets Rebekah at a well. Jacob meets Rachel at a well. Moses meets Zipporah at a well. The pattern is so consistent that a first-century Jewish reader would have understood immediately what John was doing.When Jesus arrives at a wedding in Cana and provides the wine that the bridegroom failed to supply, He is assuming the role of the true Bridegroom — the one the prophets had promised would come to claim His bride. Mary's role in this scene further establishes the typology: she functions as the new Eve, the mother of the new Adam, interceding on behalf of those in need. Her words to the servants — "Do whatever he tells you" (John 2:5) — are a deliberate echo of the obedience that Eve failed to render.Why Not Moses and Isaac?The "new Moses" typology is real and deeply present in the New Testament, but it is primarily a Matthean construction. Matthew structures his Gospel around five great discourses that parallel the five books of the Torah, presenting Jesus as the new lawgiver ascending a new Sinai. John is doing something different. His Gospel is oriented not toward Sinai but toward Eden and the Wedding Feast — not toward the giving of the Law but toward the restoration of creation and the fulfillment of the spousal covenant.The "new Isaac" typology — centered on the Aqedah, the Binding of Isaac in Genesis 22 — is theologically profound and indeed points to the Passion. But it is not the operative typology of John 1–2. Bergsma is asking us, in this question, to read attentively — to notice which Old Testament figures John is actually invoking, rather than importing frameworks from other parts of the New Testament canon.The answer is False: in the context of Episode 2 and John's Gospel as a whole, Jesus is presented as the new Adam and the eschatological Bridegroom — not primarily as the new Isaac or the new Moses.True or False: The Prologue of John's Gospel is closely tied to the theme of creation found in the opening chapter of Exodus. a. True b. False This question tests something deceptively simple: attentiveness to which book of the Old Testament the Prologue is actually echoing. The answer is not Exodus. It is Genesis."In the Beginning" — The Echo of GenesisThe entire interpretive logic of the Prologue depends on recognizing its opening words as a deliberate citation of the very first verse of the Bible. John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word" — does not open a discussion about the Exodus, the Red Sea, the giving of the Law at Sinai, or any of the great themes of the second book of Moses. It opens with the identical phrase that opens Genesis 1:1: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth."In Hebrew, this is bereshit: the first word of the entire Torah, and the Hebrew title of the book of Genesis itself. In the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament used by the early Church, Genesis 1:1 opens with ἐν ἀρχῇ — exactly the words John chooses. This is not coincidence. It is a literary and theological declaration: what you are about to read begins where everything began.The Seven-Day StructureThe connection to Genesis 1 goes far deeper than a shared opening phrase. Dr. Bergsma draws our attention to the seven-day structure embedded in John 1:1–2:11. The narrative of John's first two chapters, carefully analyzed, unfolds across a series of days that culminate in the Wedding at Cana on "the third day" — and the total count, when the days are traced precisely, reaches seven. John is presenting the ministry of Jesus as a new week of creation, culminating in the gift of the good wine at a wedding feast — a new Sabbath joy, a new rest, a new Eden.This structural parallel to Genesis 1's seven days of creation is central to John's theological purpose. Jesus does not merely interpret or supplement the old creation. He is the agent of a new one. "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being" (John 1:3) — this is not a statement about Moses or the Exodus. It is a statement about the eternal Word who was present at the first creation and who now enters that creation to renew it from within.Why the Confusion Might AriseIt is worth noting why Exodus might seem like a plausible answer. The theme of divine glory (doxa in Greek; kavod in Hebrew) — which John invokes in the Prologue ("we have seen his glory", John 1:14) and at Cana ("he revealed his glory", John 2:11) — is indeed associated with the Exodus narrative. The divine glory filled the Tabernacle in Exodus 40:34-35. The Shekinah cloud accompanied Israel through the wilderness. John is certainly aware of this Exodus resonance, and he will draw on it throughout his Gospel.But the foundational Old Testament text for the Prologue is not Exodus 1. It is Genesis 1. The creation of light, the ordering of chaos, the breath of God hovering over the waters — these are the images that underlie John's presentation of the eternal Word. When John writes that "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14), the Greek verb ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen) — literally "pitched his tent" or "tabernacled" — does echo the Exodus Tabernacle. But this is a secondary resonance enriching an already established Genesis framework, not the primary text being cited.The answer is False: the Prologue of John's Gospel is closely tied to the theme of creation found in the opening chapter of Genesis, not Exodus.

Reading John in light of the sacraments has the power to transform the way we experience and share the Good News of salvation history. In the second half of this episode, Dr. Bergsma examines John 1 and 2, investigating how Our Lord fulfills the promises of Scripture. As you read through this passage, pay close attention to Mary's humility, the swift obedience of the servants, and the trust that the steward puts in Jesus. Write down two or three practical ways you could apply what you see to your own relationship with the Lord. As you go about your week, return to your list and reflect on what you wrote.My notes:Episode 3 — Jesus Christ, Divine BridegroomDr. Bergsma shares powerful truths about Jesus' love for us and explores Our Lord's messianic role as the Divine Bridegroom of Israel.

item.description: Jesus Christ, Divine Bridegroom Scripture Focus: John 4:1–42This week, try doing lectio divina prayer with the story of the Samaritan woman (John 4:1–41). Ask the Holy Spirit to help you listen to God's voice. Read slowly through the passage as many times as you need. When you encounter a word or phrase that stands out to you, pause and meditate on it. Enter into loving conversation with the Lord. Talk to Him openly and honestly about what you notice coming up in your heart as you reflect on this story.Lectio divina — Latin for "sacred reading" — is one of the oldest and most venerable forms of prayer in the Catholic tradition. Rooted in the practice of the Desert Fathers and systematized by St. Benedict in the sixth century, it was described by the twelfth-century monk Guigo II as a ladder of four rungs by which the soul ascends toward God:1. Lectio — Reading Read the passage slowly and attentively, as though hearing it for the first time. This is not study — it is listening. Read aloud if possible. Let the words land. When a word, phrase, or image arrests your attention, stop. You do not need to finish the passage. The Holy Spirit has something to say to you there.2. Meditatio — Meditation Remain with the word or phrase that caught your attention. Repeat it gently, turn it over in your mind, allow it to descend from the head into the heart. Ask: Why does this word stand out to me? What is God showing me through it? What does it reveal about His heart — or mine?3. Oratio — Prayer Respond to God from the heart. This is conversation, not performance. Tell Him honestly what you are feeling — confusion, longing, gratitude, resistance, joy. The Samaritan woman spoke to Jesus plainly and imperfectly, and He received every word. So will He receive yours.4. Contemplatio — Contemplation Rest. Allow yourself to simply be in God's presence without words or effort. This is the gift that the other three movements prepare us for — a quiet, loving awareness of the One who is already present.Note: Do not feel pressure to move through all four stages in a single sitting. Sometimes the Spirit holds you at Lectio for the entire time. This is not failure — it is fidelity to where God is working.Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love. Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth.O God, who by the light of the Holy Spirit did instruct the hearts of the faithful, grant that by the same Holy Spirit we may be truly wise and ever enjoy His consolations. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.New American Bible, Revised Edition (NABRE)1 Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John 2 (although Jesus himself was not baptizing, just his disciples), 3 he left Judea and returned to Galilee.The Samaritan Woman4 He had to pass through Samaria. 5 So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of land that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. 6 Jacob's well was there. Jesus, tired from his journey, sat down there at the well. It was about noon.7 A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink." 8 His disciples had gone into the town to buy food. 9 The Samaritan woman said to him, "How can you, a Jew, ask me, a Samaritan woman, for a drink?" (For Jews use nothing in common with Samaritans.) 10 Jesus answered and said to her, "If you knew the gift of God and who is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him and he would have given you living water."11 The woman said to him, "Sir, you do not even have a bucket and the well is deep; where then can you get this living water? 12 Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself with his children and his flocks?" 13 Jesus answered and said to her, "Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again; 14 but whoever drinks the water I shall give will never thirst; the water I shall give will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life." 15 The woman said to him, "Sir, give me this water, so that I may not be thirsty or have to keep coming here to draw water."16 Jesus said to her, "Go call your husband and come back." 17 The woman answered and said to him, "I do not have a husband." Jesus answered her, "You are right in saying, 'I do not have a husband.' 18 For you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband. What you have said is true." 19 The woman said to him, "Sir, I can see that you are a prophet. 20 Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain; but you people say that the place to worship is in Jerusalem."21 Jesus said to her, "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. 22 You people worship what you do not understand; we worship what we understand, because salvation is from the Jews. 23 But the hour is coming, and is now here, when true worshipers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth; and indeed the Father seeks such people to worship him. 24 God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in Spirit and truth." 25 The woman said to him, "I know that the Messiah is coming, the one called the Anointed; when he comes, he will tell us everything." 26 Jesus said to her, "I am he, the one who is speaking with you."27 At that moment his disciples returned, and were amazed that he was talking with a woman, but still no one said, "What are you looking for?" or "Why are you talking with her?" 28 The woman left her water jar and went into the town and said to the people, 29 "Come see a man who told me everything I have done. Could he possibly be the Messiah?" 30 They went out of the town and came to him.31 Meanwhile, the disciples urged him, "Rabbi, eat." 32 But he said to them, "I have food to eat of which you do not know." 33 So the disciples said to one another, "Could someone have brought him something to eat?" 34 Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to finish his work. 35 Do you not say, 'In four months the harvest will be here'? I tell you, look up and see the fields ripe for the harvest. 36 The reaper is already receiving his payment and gathering crops for eternal life, so that the sower and reaper can rejoice together. 37 For here the saying is verified that 'One sows and another reaps.' 38 I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the work, and you are sharing the fruits of their work."39 Many of the Samaritans of that town began to believe in him because of the word of the woman who testified, "He told me everything I have done." 40 When the Samaritans came to him, they invited him to stay with them; and he stayed there two days. 41 Many more began to believe in him because of his word, 42 and they said to the woman, "We no longer believe because of your word; for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the savior of the world."The word or phrase that stood out to me:What I noticed in my heart as I sat with it:What I said to the Lord (Oratio):What I received in the quiet (Contemplatio):

item.title: 03 - reflection
item.description: Jesus Christ, Divine Bridegroom Scripture Focus: John 3–5Every year on the Third Sunday in Lent, the Church invites the faithful to reflect on the story of the woman at the well. In light of what Dr. Bergsma shared in this episode, why do you think the Church returns to this passage year after year? What aspects of the Samaritan woman's story reflect the themes of the Lenten season?The Church is never arbitrary in her liturgical choices. When she returns to a text year after year — and she has done so for centuries — it is because she has discerned in that text an inexhaustible depth of spiritual nourishment suited to a particular moment in the sacred year. The story of the Samaritan woman at Jacob's Well (John 4:1–42) is one of the most theologically dense passages in all of Sacred Scripture, and its placement on the Third Sunday of Lent is an act of profound pastoral wisdom.The Lenten Context: Preparation for BaptismTo understand why the Church chooses this passage for Lent, we must first recall what Lent actually is. It is not, at its origins, merely a season of personal penance for the already baptized. Its ancient heart is catechumenal — it is the final and most intense stage of preparation for those who will receive Baptism at the Easter Vigil. The Third, Fourth, and Fifth Sundays of Lent in Year A of the lectionary correspond to the three great scrutinies — solemn rites of purification and enlightenment celebrated with the elect, those preparing to enter the Church.The scrutinies are precisely what the name suggests: an honest examination, before God and the community, of the condition of the soul. They are a laying bare of interior darkness so that it might be driven out and replaced with the light of Christ. And there is no better icon of this movement in all of Scripture than the Samaritan woman.She comes to the well alone, at noon — the sixth hour, when the sun is highest and shadows are shortest. Some commentators have seen in this detail the opposite of Nicodemus: she comes in full light, but her life is one of hidden darkness. She has been drawing water alone, likely because the shame of her history has made her an outcast from the company of the other women who would come at dawn. She is isolated by sin, just as every soul preparing for Baptism must come to recognize their isolation from God through the weight of sin.The Dynamics of ConversionWhat unfolds at the well is a masterclass in the dynamics of conversion — which is why the Church, in her wisdom, returns to it every year. Jesus does not begin with accusation. He begins with thirst: "Give me a drink" (John 4:7). He enters the woman's world, meets her where she is, and draws her into conversation. This is the pattern of divine grace: it does not overwhelm but invites, not condemns but reveals.As the conversation deepens, Jesus gently brings her to the point of self-knowledge. "Go, call your husband" (John 4:16). He already knows the answer. He is not gathering information — He is inviting her to honesty, to the same interior examination that the scrutinies demand of the elect. And she responds, to her credit, with a kind of courageous half-truth: "I have no husband." Jesus honors the truth in her words and fills in what she left unspoken.This movement — from evasion to acknowledgment, from the surface to the depths — is the essential movement of Lent. It is the movement of metanoia, the Greek word the Church uses for repentance, meaning not merely feeling sorry but a turning of the mind, a reorientation of the whole person toward God.Thirst as the Lenten ConditionAt the deepest level, the story of the Samaritan woman is a story about thirst. She comes to the well because she is physically thirsty. But Jesus diagnoses a deeper thirst beneath the surface — the thirst of a soul that has been seeking in all the wrong places the one thing that can satisfy: living communion with the living God."Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again." (John 4:13–14)This is one of the most penetrating lines in the Gospel. It is a description of every human life lived without God. We keep returning to the same wells — pleasure, approval, comfort, distraction — and they keep running dry. The woman has had five husbands. She has tried again and again to fill the aching void at the center of her life. And Jesus meets her in that exhaustion with an offer that changes everything.Lent is the season when the Church asks us to sit with our thirst. To stop filling ourselves with things that do not satisfy and allow ourselves to feel, honestly, how deep the longing goes. The Samaritan woman is our companion in this. Her transformation — from isolated, shame-ridden outcast to the first evangelist of her village — is the promise of what Lent, lived well, can accomplish in each of us.Baptismal TypologyFinally, we cannot miss the sacramental dimension. The Catechism of the Catholic Church identifies water, from the very first pages of Genesis, as a primary symbol of the Holy Spirit's action (CCC 694). The living water Jesus offers the Samaritan woman is, as He Himself will make explicit in John 7:38–39, the Holy Spirit. And the Holy Spirit is given preeminently in Baptism.The Church places this passage before her catechumens in the final weeks before their Baptism because it is a portrait of what is about to happen to them. They, like the woman, are about to receive living water. They, like her, will be known completely by the One who gives it — and loved completely in that knowledge. And they, like her, will be sent to proclaim what they have received.What are your thoughts on the connection between the "living water" Jesus offers the Samaritan woman and the description of Solomon's bride as a "well of living water" in Song of Songs 4:15?The connection between John 4 and Song of Songs 4:15 is one of the most beautiful instances of typological fulfillment in all of Scripture, and it has not been lost on the great tradition of Catholic biblical interpretation.The Text of Song of SongsIn Song of Songs 4:15, the bridegroom Solomon addresses his bride with an extraordinary image: "A garden fountain, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon." The bride herself is described as a source of living water. She is the well from which the bridegroom draws life and refreshment. The entire section (4:12–5:1) describes the bride as a locked garden, a sealed fountain — an image of purity, abundance, and the intimate exclusivity of the covenant bond. She is, for her bridegroom, the source of everything he needs.The Church, following the great Origen in his Commentary on the Song of Songs, has always read this text on multiple levels simultaneously. At the literal level, it is a love poem celebrating human marriage. But at the deeper allegorical level — and the Fathers are unanimous that this deeper reading is the text's primary spiritual meaning — the bridegroom is God, and the bride is Israel and, by extension, the Church and the individual soul.The Inversion and Its MeaningNow consider what happens in John 4. Jesus, the Divine Bridegroom, comes to the Samaritan woman — a daughter of the lost Northern Kingdom, a figure of Israel's scattered and wayward Bride — at a well. And He does not draw water from her. Instead, He offers her living water from Himself.Here is the profound inversion that the typology makes visible: in Song of Songs, the bride is the well of living water for the bridegroom. In John 4, the Bridegroom offers living water to a bride who has run completely dry.This is not a contradiction but a fulfillment. It shows us the precise nature of what sin has done to Israel — and to every human soul. The bride who was meant, in God's original design, to be a garden fountain, a well of living water, has become instead a woman returning daily to an earthly well, drawing water that cannot satisfy. The image of the Song has been shattered by the history of human faithlessness.And so the Divine Bridegroom comes — not to condemn the broken image, but to restore it. He offers her the living water that will become in her "a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:14). He is not taking from her. He is giving her back what she was always meant to be.The Holy Spirit as Living WaterJesus identifies this living water explicitly with the Holy Spirit in John 7:38–39: "Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.' Now this he said about the Spirit." The Holy Spirit is the living water of the New Covenant. And the reception of the Holy Spirit — particularly in Baptism and Confirmation — restores to the soul what sin had taken away: the capacity to be, in the language of Song of Songs, a garden fountain, a source of living water for others.This is what the Samaritan woman becomes. She receives the living water from Jesus. She returns to her village. And from her flows the evangelistic proclamation that brings her whole community to Christ. She is transformed, by encounter with the Bridegroom, from a dry and isolated woman into the very thing Solomon celebrated in his bride: a well of living water for those around her.The Cross as the Deepest FulfillmentWe cannot close this reflection without noting that the ultimate source of this living water is the pierced side of Christ on Calvary. John tells us with deliberate solemnity: "one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out" (John 19:34). The Church Fathers — Augustine most memorably — saw in this the birth of the Church from the side of the New Adam, just as Eve was drawn from the side of the first Adam. The living water that flows from Christ's wounded side is the water of Baptism, and the blood is the Eucharist.The Bridegroom gives Himself entirely for His Bride. He becomes, on the Cross, the inexhaustible well of living water that His Bride was always meant to be.Dr. Bergsma described the man Jesus healed in John 5 as an "icon of the people of Israel." When you examine this passage, what dimensions of the paralyzed man's story reflect the history of the Israelites in the Old Testament? What aspects of the man's encounter with Our Lord can offer insight into the Christian life today?The healing of the paralytic at the Pool of Bethesda (John 5:1–15) is, on the surface, a straightforward miracle story. But once we read it with the eyes of the tradition — trained to see how the New Testament is the Old Testament unveiled — it becomes something far more: a compressed retelling of Israel's entire salvation history, and a mirror held up to the condition of every human soul in need of God's healing grace.The Number 38: An Unmistakable SignalJohn tells us that the man had been lying by the pool for thirty-eight years. This number is not chosen at random. For a reader steeped in the Old Testament, it would have resonated immediately with one of the most painful passages in the Pentateuch.In Deuteronomy 2:14, Moses recalls the years of Israel's wandering and notes: "And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the Lord had sworn to them." Thirty-eight years: the precise duration of Israel's punishment in the desert, the period during which the faithless generation that refused to enter the Promised Land was consigned to paralysis, to going nowhere, to waiting for death while the next generation grew up. The paralytic has been lying by the pool for exactly this length of time. John is waving a flag for his theologically literate readers: this man is Israel.The Pool and the LawThe Pool of Bethesda had five porticoes — and lying under those five porticoes were the multitudes of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the paralyzed, waiting for the water to be stirred. The Church Fathers, including Tertullian and later commentators, noted that five porticoes correspond to the five books of Moses — the Torah. Under the canopy of the Law, Israel lay sick and waiting.This is a precise theological statement about the limits of the Mosaic Law. The Law, as St. Paul will later articulate with such force in his letters to the Romans and Galatians, was never designed to justify — to save — but to diagnose. It revealed the condition of sin but could not heal it. The paralytic lies under five porticoes, waiting. The Law surrounds him. But the Law cannot make him rise.Helplessness and the Need for a SaviorThe most piercing moment of this story is the paralytic's answer to Jesus's question: "Do you want to be healed?" (John 5:6). We might expect a simple yes. Instead, we get a lament: "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me." (John 5:7) He has no one. Thirty-eight years, and no one has helped him. He is utterly dependent on others and utterly abandoned by them. This is Israel in Egypt — enslaved, powerless, unable to save themselves, with no deliverer in sight. It is Israel in the desert — unable to enter the land, incapable of claiming what God had promised. And in a deeper sense, it is every human soul in the condition of sin: paralyzed, unable to rise by its own power, perpetually displaced by those more agile or more favored, waiting for a healing that never comes.This helplessness is not incidental. It is the very condition that makes the miracle possible — and that makes its meaning legible. Jesus does not come to those who have managed to limp to the pool on their own. He comes to the one who has been lying there the longest, who has the least hope, who has no one."Rise, Take Up Your Mat, and Walk"Jesus does not ask for effort or merit. He commands. "Rise, take up your bed, and walk" (John 5:8). Three imperatives. And the man rises.This is the new Exodus. Moses stretched out his staff; the sea parted. Jesus speaks, and a man paralyzed for thirty-eight years stands upright and walks. He is, in his person, the crossing of the Jordan — the end of the long paralysis, the entry into the land that could not be achieved under the Law. What the five porticoes could not accomplish, a single word from the Son of God accomplishes instantly.The Catechism, in its treatment of the Sacrament of Penance, notes that the healings of Jesus in the Gospels are signs of the forgiveness and restoration that He confers through the sacraments of the Church (CCC 1503–1504). The study guide itself draws the explicit connection: the healing of the paralytic points to the Sacrament of Reconciliation. This is not an imposition but a recognition. Jesus's final word to the man — "Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you" (John 5:14) — makes the connection between the physical healing and the interior healing of the soul undeniable.The Man's Response: A WarningWe cannot idealize the paralytic's response. When the Jewish authorities confront him about carrying his mat on the Sabbath, he deflects responsibility: "The man who healed me told me to" (John 5:11). And then, upon learning that his healer is Jesus, he goes and reports this to those who are seeking to persecute Him (John 5:15).This, too, mirrors Israel's history — the pattern of receiving grace and failing to respond with corresponding gratitude and fidelity. The healed man does not seek out his healer to give thanks. He does not follow Him. He does not become a disciple. And in this he stands as a warning to all of us who receive the grace of the sacraments and then drift back into old habits, old paralysis, old indifference.Application for the Christian LifeThe man's story is our story. There are areas of every Christian life that have been paralyzed for years — perhaps decades. Sins we have confessed and returned to. Wounds we have carried so long we have come to regard them as permanent. Interior attitudes that have kept us lying by the same pool, watching others receive what we cannot seem to reach.Jesus asks us the same question He asked the paralytic: "Do you want to be healed?" It is a more searching question than it appears. Sometimes our paralysis has become our identity. We are not sure who we would be without it. The healing Jesus offers requires that we rise — that we actually pick up our mat and walk, leaving behind the place where we have been lying for so long.The Sacrament of Reconciliation is the privileged place where this encounter happens. The priest, acting in persona Christi, speaks the words of absolution — and Christ speaks through them as surely as He spoke to the paralytic by the pool. The thirty-eight years of waiting can end in a single moment of grace.But the grace demands a response. "Sin no more." To receive the healing of Reconciliation and return to the same sin is to act as the paralytic did — to take the gift and walk away from the Giver. The Christian life is not a series of returns to the pool but a sustained walking: the daily choosing, in cooperation with grace, to remain upright, to remain free, to remain in the company of the One who first commanded us to rise.

item.title: 02- review
item.description: Jesus Christ, Divine Bridegroom Scripture Focus: John 3–5In John 3:1-2, Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night. What does this action symbolize? a. A lack of knowledge b. The light of the Holy Spirit c. Spiritual darkness d. Both A & C To understand why Nicodemus coming "by night" carries such weight, we must first appreciate the literary and theological architecture of John's Gospel. From the very opening of the Prologue, St. John establishes a governing cosmic opposition: light and darkness. "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it." (John 1:5) This is not merely poetic atmosphere. For John, light and darkness are moral and spiritual categories. Light is identified with Christ Himself — "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12) — and with the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit. Darkness, by contrast, is the condition of the soul that has not yet received that illumination. It is the natural habitat of sin, ignorance, and unbelief.When John tells us that Nicodemus came to Jesus by night, he is doing something the Church Fathers recognized immediately: he is placing Nicodemus squarely within the realm of darkness — not as a moral condemnation, but as a theological statement about his current spiritual condition.Darkness as Spiritual Blindness (option C)Nicodemus is a Pharisee and "a ruler of the Jews" — a man of considerable religious standing. He even acknowledges that Jesus comes from God ("no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him", John 3:2). And yet, for all his religious learning, he remains in the dark. He has not yet come to faith. He approaches Jesus secretly, under cover of night, because the full light of revelation has not yet pierced his heart.St. Augustine, commenting on this passage, notes that Nicodemus represents those souls who possess a kind of preliminary faith — they see the signs, they sense the divine presence — but have not yet made the full passage from darkness to light. He writes that Nicodemus "came to Jesus, but came by night; that is, he came to the Light, but came in darkness." The darkness is not merely external. It is the condition of his interior life at that moment.Darkness as Lack of Understanding (option A)This same darkness is expressed immediately in what follows. When Jesus tells Nicodemus that "unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3), Nicodemus responds with a question that reveals how deeply carnal — how earthbound — his thinking still is: "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" (John 3:4).He hears the words of eternal life and interprets them biologically. He stands before the Word made flesh and cannot yet read the language of the Spirit. This is precisely the lack of knowledge that the darkness symbolizes. His mind is not yet illumined by grace, and so the spiritual realities Jesus speaks of remain opaque to him.St. Cyril of Alexandria draws the same connection: Nicodemus's inability to understand spiritual rebirth flows from the very darkness he carries into the encounter. Knowledge and light, in Johannine theology, are inseparable. To be in darkness is to be without true understanding.Why not option B?Option B — "the light of the Holy Spirit" — is precisely the opposite of what the night represents. The Holy Spirit is the agent of illumination, the one who leads us into all truth (John 16:13). To come by night is to come before that illumination has taken hold. It is the absence of the Holy Spirit's light, not its presence.The Catechism and Baptismal TypologyIt is worth noting that the Church has always read this passage in close connection with the Sacrament of Baptism. The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that Baptism is the sacrament of illumination (CCC 1216), drawing directly on the early Christian title for Baptism: photismos — enlightenment. To be baptized is to pass from darkness into the marvelous light of Christ (1 Peter 2:9).Nicodemus's night visit, then, is not merely a narrative detail. It is a theological portrait of the soul before Baptism — dwelling in spiritual darkness and ignorance, yet drawn nonetheless toward the Light. Jesus does not send him away. He meets him in the darkness and speaks to him of water and the Spirit (John 3:5). The very conversation foreshadows what Baptism will accomplish: the passage from night into light, from ignorance into knowledge, from death into new life.True or False: The Samaritan woman's adultery is symbolic of the idolatrous history of the Northern tribes.At first reading, the encounter at Jacob's Well in John 4 appears to be a straightforward story of personal conversion: a woman with a troubled past meets Jesus, comes to recognize Him as the Messiah, and runs to tell her village. And it is certainly that. But the Catholic tradition, following the method of the Church Fathers and rooted in the deep logic of salvation history, recognizes that John has embedded a far richer meaning in the detail that the woman has had five husbands — and that the man she currently lives with is not her husband.The Historical Key: 2 Kings 17To grasp the symbolism, we must go back to one of the most consequential events in Israel's history: the fall of the Northern Kingdom of Samaria to the Assyrian Empire in 722 BC. The Assyrian policy was to displace conquered populations. When they deported the Israelites of the North, they repopulated the land with five foreign nations: "And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel." (2 Kings 17:24) Each of these five nations brought its own gods. item.title: this is IT
item.description: Approaches and suggestions for defining Information TechnologyRestricting IT to computers is a common but historically shallow framing. It ignores the decades of foundational work that made computing possible — and the broader truth that information, not hardware, is the subject. The better question is: what does IT do? It captures, processes, stores, transmits, and retrieves information. The machinery changes; the mission doesn't.Define IT by what it does, not what it is made of: Any technology whose primary purpose is to handle information — acquiring, storing, processing, transmitting, or displaying it. This immediately includes: Telegraphs and telephone switches Radio and television broadcasting infrastructure Punch card systems (pre-electronic) Modern computing, networking, and AI Why this works: It's technology-agnostic and future-proof. When something new arrives (quantum computing, biological computing), you can ask "does it handle information?" rather than "does it look like a computer?"Trace IT back to its intellectual origins rather than its commercial ones.Key waypoints: 1840s — Telegraph: the first system to separate information from a physical carrier (the message from the messenger) 1876 — Telephone: real-time voice as data Bell Labs (1920s–1970s) — Transistor, information theory, Shannon's entropy, error correction, signal processing. This is arguably the true birthplace of modern IT 1948 — Claude Shannon's A Mathematical Theory of Communication — the foundational paper that defines information mathematically and underpins all digital systems 1950s–60s — Mainframe computing emerges from this lineage, not apart from it 1970s–present — Personal computing, internet, mobile, cloud The takeaway: computers didn't create IT; IT created computers. The field existed before the transistor.Information technology is a subset of the broader field of information science, which includes: How information is structured and classified (library science, ontologies, metadata) How it is communicated (linguistics, semiotics, media studies) How it is secured and controlled (cryptography, policy) How it is used by humans (HCI, cognitive science) This approach connects IT to disciplines that don't typically appear in a CS curriculum but are inseparable from it in practice. Cybersecurity, UX, data governance, and AI ethics all live here.IT doesn't exist in isolation — it's always embedded in social systems. Defining it purely as hardware or software misses the human layer. IT is the ensemble of tools, practices, standards, and institutions that societies use to manage information. This includes: Postal systems (organised information routing) Filing and records management Standards bodies (IEEE, IETF, ISO) — the "invisible infrastructure" Data centres as physical/social infrastructure Why this is useful for teaching: It prevents students from thinking of IT as purely technical, which helps when addressing ethics, policy, and real-world impact.For a more rigorous framing: information, in the technical sense, is reduction of uncertainty. IT is any system that does this systematically.A traffic light is a rudimentary IT system. A spreadsheet is an IT system. So is a filing cabinet. What makes modern IT distinctive is: Scale (billions of operations, billions of users) Speed (real-time or near-real-time) Programmability (the system can be reconfigured without physical change) This framing lets you distinguish IT from other technologies while explaining why electronics and software became central — they maximise all three properties.Rather than one rigid definition, consider a layered scope:The "core" is what most people mean by IT in everyday use. The outer layers are what separate a practitioner from a technician. Open with Bell Labs — it's one of the most productive research environments in history and draws a direct line from physics → information theory → computing → the internet. It immediately challenges the "IT = computers" assumption. Use Shannon's definition of information as an early anchor. It's rigorous, non-circular, and gives students a durable mental model that survives technological change. Include one non-digital case study (e.g., the London postal system in the 1800s, or telephone exchange operators) to demonstrate that information systems predate electronics. Acknowledge the fuzzy boundary — IT overlaps with electrical engineering, communications, media, and management. That's not a weakness; it's evidence that information is genuinely central to modern life. Document created: 2026-02-26

item.title: discussion-01
item.description:
A working discussion space for figuring out how the ITHS Curation Committee should approach: Defining the structure of an ontology for IT historical artifacts, people, and relationships Translating that ontology into a database architecture Running the process collaboratively as a group (not just technically) An ontology for a historical society isn't just a schema. It's a set of claims about what kinds of things exist, how they relate, and what the organization believes is worth tracking. Before touching any database tool, the committee needs to answer questions like: What is the primary unit of record? (An artifact? A product line? A company? A person? An event?) What does "historical significance" mean for this organization? (Who decides? By what criteria?) How do we model influence and lineage? ("X led to Y" is a relationship, but there are many kinds of causality) What is the boundary between canonical record and user contribution? These are editorial and philosophical questions, not technical ones. The database follows from the answers.These examples are chosen because they faced the same core challenge: a community needed to agree on what things are before they could build anything.The Getty Research Institute maintains three controlled vocabularies — the Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT), the Union List of Artist Names (ULAN), and the Thesaurus of Geographic Names (TGN). These are among the most mature cultural heritage ontologies in existence.Relevance to ITHS: They separate concept records (what a thing is, abstractly) from instance records (a specific object or person) ULAN explicitly models relationships between artists: teacher/student, collaborator, influenced-by The AAT has a formal process for community submissions and editorial review — this maps well to the "canonical vs. user submission" problem Key lesson: They started with use cases, not with schema. "What questions do curators actually ask?" drove the structure.Reference: getty.edu/research/tools/vocabulariesWikidata is a general-purpose, community-maintained knowledge graph that underlies much of Wikipedia's structured data. Everything is a statement about an item, with properties and qualifiers.Relevance to ITHS: It explicitly handles the "X influenced Y" problem via properties like influenced by, has part, follows, followed by It has a clean separation between the item (canonical) and references (sourced claims) It's entirely open and the data model documentation is excellent for learning how to think about these problems Key lesson: Their data model evolved through community consensus via "WikiProjects" — groups that decided on the properties and structure for a domain (e.g., WikiProject Video Games, WikiProject Computing). This is a direct model for how the ITHS committee could work.
Reference: wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:WikiProjectsThe CHM has an online collection catalog that models hardware, software, people, and corporate history. They've had to solve the same "what is a canonical item?" question — is the canonical item the product design, the specific manufactured unit, or the product line?Relevance to ITHS: Their distinction between artifact (a physical thing), object type (a class of thing), and lot (a collection) maps onto the ITHS problem of personal submissions vs. canonical records They use a controlled vocabulary for significance/impact categories Key lesson: They distinguish "what the object is" from "what the object means" — physical description is separated from historical narrative. This prevents the ontology from collapsing under the weight of interpretation.
Reference: computerhistory.org/collections/Rick Prelinger's film archive and the broader Internet Archive have grappled with how to describe media items that have complex provenance chains — one film might be a copy of a copy, with annotations added by multiple hands.Relevance to ITHS: The "user submits their copy or story of a canonical item" feature is essentially a provenance and versioning problem Dublin Core and Schema.org (which IA uses heavily) are good prior art for simple, flat metadata that is still interoperable Key lesson: Don't invent what already exists. Dublin Core, Schema.org, and SKOS cover a huge amount of the basic metadata and relationship vocabulary. Start by mapping your concepts to these before creating custom properties.Open Library models the same three-tier structure that ITHS likely needs:Key lesson: This hierarchy is well-understood and worth adopting directly. It cleanly separates the abstract thing from its instantiations.
Reference: openlibrary.org/developers/apiBased on the above examples, here is a rough sequence for how the committee might work:Before any data modeling, collect 10–15 concrete questions that the database should be able to answer. Examples: "What hardware innovations came out of Xerox PARC and what products did they influence?" "Show me a timeline of storage media from punch cards to SSDs" "Who were the key engineers at DEC and what did they go on to build?" "What members have submitted photos of Apple I machines?" These become the test cases for the ontology. If a proposed schema can't answer them, it's incomplete.Working from the use cases, list the types of things and types of relationships that appear. Don't worry about the database yet. A whiteboard or a simple document is fine.Entity types might include: Person, Organization, Product, ProductLine, Concept/Innovation, Event, Document/Publication, PhysicalArtifact (user submission).Relationship types might include: EmployedBy, InventedBy, InfluencedBy, PrecededBy, PartOf, VersionOf, ContributedTo.Before designing custom schema, check if Schema.org, Wikidata properties, or the Getty AAT already have the concept. This saves time and enables future interoperability.Write entity definitions and relationship definitions in plain sentences before touching any technical notation. Example: A Product is a commercially released item (hardware or software) with a known manufacturer and release date. A Product may have a PrecededBy relationship to another Product if the earlier Product was a direct technical or commercial predecessor. Pick one domain (e.g., personal computers from 1975–1985) and build the schema for just that slice. Load a small amount of real data. See what breaks.Only after Phases 1–5 is it worth deciding: relational, graph, or hybrid? Document store? The answer should fall out of the data naturally, not be chosen up front. What is the minimum viable set of entity types to launch with? Who has editorial authority over canonical records vs. user submissions? Is the goal a public-facing database, an internal curatorial tool, or both? What existing databases (Wikidata, CHM catalog) should we link to rather than duplicate? How do we handle contested history? (Competing claims of "who invented X") Share this doc with the committee for feedback Schedule a use-case collection session (Phase 1) Identify which committee members have worked with any of the reference systems above Look at the existing Drupal 7 database schema — what entities does it already have?
